name: Fort Anchor
description:
Fort Anchor is the name the GLMZ Metropolitan Authority gave the former Great Lakes Naval Station when they converted it — or more accurately, when Ringo Defense Solutions converted it on a no-bid contract and the Metropolitan Authority signed the paperwork. The original naval training facility, which had processed American sailors for a century and a half, now processes a different kind of human traffic: climate refugees, economic migrants, and the steady flow of undocumented people moving north through the Corridor seeking entry into the upper GLMZ's marginally less catastrophic labor markets.

The processing center occupies the eastern half of the old base, a grid of repurposed barracks and administrative buildings where new arrivals are biometrically registered, neurally scanned, and assigned a provisional tier status that will determine every aspect of their life in the Corridor. Provisional Tier 1 — which is what most arrivals receive — grants the right to exist within GLMZ jurisdiction without being arrested for it. It does not grant employment authorization, medical access, or housing assistance. It grants existence. The distinction between Provisional Tier 1 and 'excluded' is technical, legal, and in practical terms, largely meaningless.

The western half of Fort Anchor is a Ringo garrison — the ground-force complement to the air and logistics operations at the Waukegan compound. Approximately 8,000 Ringo security personnel are stationed here, and their presence gives the processing center its particular character: a place where the humanitarian language of refugee assistance coexists with razor wire, automated sentry turrets, and the constant reminder that the people being 'processed' are being processed by the same company that sells weapons systems. Ringo's contract with the Metropolitan Authority specifies 'humane and orderly processing.' The contract does not define humane. The contract does not define orderly. Ringo defined both, and their definitions prioritize throughput.

The town of North Chicago — the civilian community surrounding the base — has been economically dependent on military and quasi-military installation spending since the 1940s. Nothing about that has changed except the uniform. Local businesses serve Ringo personnel. Local housing absorbs people who completed processing and couldn't afford to go anywhere else. The result is a community where the processors and the processed live side by side, eat at the same restaurants, and send their children to the same underfunded schools. The awkwardness of this is lost on no one.

sights: The processing center's intake queue — visible from the main road, a line of people that fluctuates between hundreds and thousands depending on the season
Ringo garrison vehicles moving in convoy along the base perimeter road, armored and unhurried
Biometric scanning stations at the processing center entrance, their blue lights visible at night from a kilometer away
Civilian neighborhoods pressed against the base fence line, close enough to hear the PA system announcements
Children playing in vacant lots while their parents wait in processing queues that can last days
sounds: The processing center PA system — automated announcements in twelve languages, cycling continuously
Garrison activity — vehicle engines, equipment loading, the organized noise of a military installation
The processing queue — thousands of people waiting, talking, arguing, praying, and trying to keep children calm
Local traffic along the commercial strip — the ordinary sounds of a town that exists because a base exists
The occasional sonic crack of a Ringo aerospace vehicle launching from the garrison's vertical pad
smells: Institutional food from the processing center's mass feeding operation — nutritionally adequate, culinarily punitive
Vehicle exhaust from the garrison — Ringo runs hydrogen fuel cells but the support fleet still burns synth-diesel
The particular smell of too many people in too small a space, drifting from the intake barracks on warm days
atmosphere.feel: A place where bureaucracy and human desperation have reached a stable equilibrium. Fort Anchor processes people with the efficiency of a logistics operation, because that is what it is. The humanitarian framing is not entirely false — people are fed, scanned, documented, and released into a system that will largely ignore them. The alternative is not being processed at all, which means not existing in any system, which means the ungoverned corridors. Fort Anchor is better than the alternative. This is the most damning thing about it.

demographics: Permanent population approximately 45,000. Transient processing population fluctuates between 5,000-20,000 at any given time. Permanent residents are predominantly Tier 1-2, split between Ringo personnel families and settled former refugees. The processed population is drawn from every displacement crisis of the last thirty years: Gulf Coast, Central American climate corridor, Pacific Island submersion, and the ongoing internal displacement from the Dust Belt.
economy: Ringo garrison spending drives the local economy. Processing center support contracts. Small-business service economy catering to base personnel. The informal economy among the processed population is survival-based: barter, labor exchange, and the careful hoarding of whatever resources arrive.
power_structure: Ringo holds effective authority over the entire district through its garrison command and processing center contract. The GLMZ Metropolitan Authority maintains a liaison office that rubber-stamps Ringo's operational decisions. Local civilian government exists but operates within parameters Ringo defines. The processed population has no political representation of any kind.
dangers: Ringo automated security — the perimeter systems do not distinguish between threats and confused civilians
Processing delays — being stuck in the intake system for weeks or months, with no legal recourse and diminishing resources
Exploitation of the processed — labor trafficking, organ harvesting, and neural interface theft targeting people with no documentation and no advocates
Garrison personnel off-duty behavior — not all Ringo employees handle the moral weight of their work gracefully
Data vulnerability — biometric and neural scan data from processing is stored on Ringo servers with Ringo's definition of privacy
opportunities: Intelligence on Ringo operations — the processing center is Ringo's most visible and least secure operation
Humanitarian contacts — the NGO workers and aid organizations operating at Fort Anchor are connected to networks throughout the GLMZ
Identity documentation — the processing system creates identities, and any system that creates identities can be exploited
Recruitment — the processed population includes skilled people from every profession, available for any work that offers a path forward
story_hooks: A batch of processing records has been altered — someone inside Ringo is creating false identities for people who were never processed, and the question is whether this is corruption or mercy
A former Ringo processing officer has gone public with testimony about 'expedited disposition' protocols for arrivals flagged by NeoCortex's pattern recognition systems
Someone Kyle knew before — from before the story starts — appears in the processing queue
frequented_by: Ringo garrison personnel and their families
Refugees and migrants in various stages of processing
NGO workers, legal aid volunteers, and humanitarian contractors
Fixers who recruit from the processed population — some offering legitimate work, some not
